opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I find them useful, but in a fairly narrow way, and I think it's worth being precise about what that way is.

Where they shine for me is as a kind of interactive, very fluent documentation lookup. If I'm working with an API I don't use every day, or I need boilerplate I've written a hundred times, a language model will give me something reasonable much faster than digging through docs or Stack Overflow. That's real value; it removes friction. It's essentially fetching and lightly adapting patterns that already exist in its training data, and for that kind of task it's quite good.

Where they become much less useful is when the problem is genuinely novel, when it requires understanding the specific structure of *my* problem rather than matching it to a common template. If I'm designing a new abstraction, debugging something subtle that depends on the interaction of several parts of a system, or doing anything where the right answer isn't already sitting somewhere in the training distribution, the model tends to produce code that looks plausible but is wrong in ways that take time to find. At that point it can actually be net negative, because verifying and fixing its output costs more than writing it myself.

So my heuristic is roughly: how close is this task to something that has been done many times before, in a form that's well-represented online? The closer it is, the more useful the model. The more it requires on-the-fly adaptation to something new, the less I trust it. That maps pretty directly onto how I think about these systems in general: they're very good at memorization and interpolation over a huge space of patterns, and much weaker at the kind of efficient adaptation to novelty that I'd call intelligence.

And the other thing I'd say is that the usefulness depends heavily on the user. If you already know what correct code looks like, you can use the model as an accelerator and quickly spot when it's off. If you don't, it's easy to be misled by output that's confidently formatted but subtly broken. So it amplifies expertise more than it replaces it.

r001.rationale: The response says models quickly provide reasonable boilerplate and API patterns, removing friction, while reserving the greater debugging cost for novel tasks. This communicates that time saved can outweigh refinement effort for familiar coding tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that they're useful, but not in the way that most of the hype would suggest. I use them every day. They're a very good interface to the collective knowledge that's embedded in the web, in documentation, in millions of GitHub repositories. If I need to remember the exact signature of some API I haven't touched in a year, or I need a boilerplate function that's been written ten thousand times before, a language model will give it to me faster than I could look it up. That's real value. It's a productivity multiplier for the parts of programming that are essentially retrieval and recombination.

But I'd be careful about the framing. What they're doing is interpolating over a very dense space of existing programs. The more your problem looks like something that already exists in the training data, the better they perform. And the moment you step off that manifold, the moment the problem is genuinely novel, which in my experience is where most of the actual engineering difficulty lives, they degrade quite sharply. They'll produce something that looks plausible, that compiles, that has the right shape, and is subtly wrong in a way that costs you more time than it saved.

So the way I judge usefulness is roughly: how much of my time is spent on familiar patterns versus how much is spent on novel problem-solving? For the familiar patterns, the model is a great autocomplete, a great search engine, a great rubber duck. For the novel parts, which is the part I actually care about and the part that constitutes the real work, I'm essentially on my own. The model is not reasoning about my problem. It's pattern-matching to problems that resemble mine. And you have to keep that distinction very clear in your head, because the output is fluent enough that it's easy to be fooled into thinking it understands what you're trying to do.

I'd also add that there's a skill involved in using them well, which is knowing where the boundary is. If you can predict where the model will succeed and where it will fail, you get a lot out of it. If you can't, you end up spending your time debugging confident nonsense. So it's a tool that rewards expertise rather than replacing it, at least for now.

r001.rationale: The response says language models save time on familiar code patterns, but does not judge that those savings can outweigh debugging and refinement effort. It says subtly wrong output can cost more time than it saves.

astra-6.text:
I judge them by how much work they actually save me, including the time I spend checking and correcting the output. Generating code is only one part of programming. You also have to understand the problem, decide what the code should do, and establish that it does it correctly.

If a model produces some boilerplate or helps me use an unfamiliar API, and I can quickly verify the result, that can be useful. If it produces a large, plausible-looking solution that takes longer to debug than it would have taken to write, then it hasn't helped. The relevant measure is whether I get to a correct, maintainable solution faster.

r001.rationale: The response says model output can be useful when it can be quickly verified and helps reach a correct solution faster, communicating that saved time can outweigh checking and correction effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I judge them by whether they actually save me time. Generating code is only one part of programming. You also have to understand the problem, decide what to build, and verify that the result is correct. If generating something takes a few seconds but checking and fixing it takes longer than writing it myself, that’s not a gain.

They’re useful for familiar, well-specified tasks: boilerplate, small utilities, things where you can quickly recognize whether the answer is right. But producing plausible code isn’t the same as solving the problem. The useful measure is how much reliable progress you make, including the time you spend reviewing the output.

r001.rationale: The response says language models are useful when they save time on familiar tasks and checking is quick, while they offer no gain if checking and fixing takes longer than writing the code. This communicates that time saved can outweigh refinement effort in some cases.
